one_line: A short walkthrough of React Doctor, a Rust-fast (OXLint-based) CLI that flags React anti-patterns, shown on an old personal project and an open-source CRM monorepo.
summary: Better Stack presents React Doctor, a CLI that scans React code for anti-patterns such as unnecessary useEffect, accessibility issues, prop drilling and hard-coded secrets. It runs on OXLint and builds an AST of the project to match hook usage, prop structures and component boundaries, and the speaker says it encodes 47+ React best-practice checks. Andrus runs it on a stock-chart app he wrote six years earlier and gets a near-perfect score, with three valid findings: index used as a key, Recharts loaded eagerly (suggests lazy loading), and four useState calls in one useEffect (suggests useReducer). He then runs it on the open-source Twenty CRM, where the tool detects the monorepo and reports per-package scores. The marketing site has one missing-alt error and the front package has 99 errors, which he still calls in the "green zone". The video ends by suggesting the tool for sanity-checking projects and finding places to contribute to open-source repos. It can also be run as a coding-agent skill or through a Node.js API, though the video does not demonstrate either.

key_ideas.idea: React Doctor is a CLI for detecting React anti-patterns, built on OXLint and an AST of the project.
key_ideas.detail: It looks for hook usage, prop structures and component boundaries, and the speaker says it is written against 47+ React best practices. The lint core is Rust-based, which the speaker credits for speed.

key_ideas.idea: The checks go beyond style into accessibility and security.
key_ideas.detail: Examples shown include hard-coded security keys and a loading-state pattern, with guidance on when to use it versus useTransition.

key_ideas.idea: It can be used as a skill for a coding agent or programmatically through a Node.js API.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker mentions both integration paths but does not demonstrate either in the video.

key_ideas.idea: On an old personal project, the findings were concrete and valid.
key_ideas.detail: The tool flagged index used as a list key, Recharts as a heavy dependency that should be lazy-loaded, and four useState calls in a single useEffect that should become useReducer.

key_ideas.idea: It handles monorepos by scoring each package separately.
key_ideas.detail: On the Twenty CRM repo it detected the workspace packages and produced a separate score for each, with the front package showing many more issues than the marketing site.

key_ideas.idea: The speaker's suggested use is contribution discovery as well as sanity checking.
key_ideas.detail: Because the project is open source and young, he suggests running it on other repos to find places to contribute new checks or fixes.

techniques.name: Run a React anti-pattern scan on a repo
techniques.how: Run the React Doctor CLI from the project root. The video does not show the exact command or flags, so check the project README. It returns a score plus a list of findings. In a monorepo it detects workspace packages and reports a score per package.
techniques.when: Before merging or shipping a React codebase, as a quick sanity check, or to triage an unfamiliar repo.

techniques.name: Fix the three demonstrated findings
techniques.how: 1) Replace array-index keys with stable IDs. 2) Lazy-load heavy chart libraries such as Recharts (for example with React.lazy and Suspense). 3) Collapse several related useState calls inside one useEffect into a single useReducer.
techniques.when: When a scan flags these patterns. Each fix is a common React refactor, not specific to this tool.

techniques.name: Use the scanner as a coding-agent skill
techniques.how: The speaker says React Doctor can be packaged as a skill so a coding agent can run it. He does not show setup steps.
techniques.when: When an agent is writing React code and you want its output checked against the same rules before a human reviews it.

tools: Amy (named as a creator project, caption may be imprecise)

numbers.claim: The tool checks against more than 47 React best practices.
The speaker says OXLint can scan tens of thousands of lines of code in milliseconds. This is an unmeasured claim.
A personal six-year-old stock-chart project scored nearly perfect with three findings.
The marketing-site package of Twenty CRM had 1 error, a missing alt tag.
The front package of Twenty CRM had 99 errors and was still in the green zone.

hot_takes: The title and the framing ("I thought I was a Senior React Dev") are clickbait. The video is a 4.5-minute tour of one tool with no comparison to existing React linting options such as eslint-plugin-react.
The speed claim (tens of thousands of lines in milliseconds) is asserted, not benchmarked on screen.
The score scale and the 'green zone' threshold are never explained, so the reader cannot tell how to interpret 99 errors.
The video shows a demo of findings, not a reproducible setup. The exact install and run commands and the skill and Node API integrations are left out.
The tool is described as open source and young, so rule quality and false-positive rate are unknown from this video alone.

relevance.why: A frontend React linter has no fit with the proxy, memory, inference, sandbox or observability layers of AgentOS.

ProsHarness wraps Claude Code, and a fast deterministic scanner could be one of the quality checks run on agent-written React code. The video shows it can be used as an agent skill, but it demonstrates nothing about agent workflows.
relevance.action: If a ProsHarness run touches React code, consider a skill that runs a deterministic React scanner as a gate after the agent's edits and before its plan-critique step.
